title: kv-eviction-algorithm-telemetry-correlation-journal
content:
Purpose and high level

This is a running lab journal documenting experiments that correlate eviction algorithm behavior with runtime telemetry signals (reuse rates, memory bandwidth, paging events, and tail latency). Goal: find low-effort heuristics (and corresponding telemetry hooks) that reduce paging-induced stalls while keeping high reuse for typical LLM inference workloads.

Background / motivation

We've seen recurring production incidents where KV cache thrashing + paging spikes cause token latency climbs and a cascade of request queuing. Current LRU-style eviction and a global recency counter are simple, but they don't account for cross-request reuse patterns or instantaneous memory bandwidth pressure. Hypothesis: combining short-term reuse signals with bandwidth-aware eviction thresholds can reduce tail latency with small throughput cost.

What I'm tracking in this doc

- experiments tried (date, config, short result)
- telemetry signals used and how measured (samplers, perf counters)
- correlation analyses and ad-hoc plots (described in words)
- follow-ups, action items, and TODOs

Test harness and workload

- Model: 7B transformer (decoder-only) with long-prefix chat sessions (average seq len 1024, max 4096 for some tests).
- Node: NVMe-backed instance, 8xA100 40GB equivalent; memory pressure set to create realistic KV spill-to-dram scenarios.
- Concurrency: 120 concurrent requests for stress runs, 20 for baseline functional tests.
- Synthetic workload: mixed traffic (50% short prompts <128 tokens, 30% medium 256-1024, 20% long >1024).
- Real workload: anonymized sample from hosted-api production replay (day-of-week = Tues, heavy chat traffic).

Telemetry signals collected

1) KV reuse counter (per-key reuse since last epoch) sampled at 1s resolution.
2) KV touch heatmap: short histogram of reuse distance (0-1s, 1-10s, 10-60s, >60s).
3) Memory bandwidth util (% of sustained DMA BW) from perf counters (sampled at 100ms).
4) Page faults (minor/major) and swap activity logs (system counters + runtime pageback traces).
5) Eviction events: timestamped with reason (age, capacity, manual) and bytes evicted.
6) Request-level latency (p50/p95/p99), and tokens-per-second per GPU.

Measurement methodology notes

- To avoid perturbing the system, reuse counters are kept lightweight: sampled aggregates, not per-request full traces. We also perform a small number of instrumented runs with detailed traces for causality checks.
- Bandwidth is noisy; we smooth with 1s rolling windows and compare against baseline idle curves.
- When we report paging correlation we use a 5s causal window: eviction spike -> bandwidth increase -> page faults within 0-5s.

Experiment log (selected entries)

2024-09-16: baseline-LRU
- Config: standard LRU eviction, TTL disabled, no prefetch.
- Observations: steady-state p50=18ms, p95=82ms, p99=310ms. During synthetic long requests p99 rose to 720ms with NVMe read spikes. KV churn high: eviction rate ~420MB/s during peak.
- Conclusion: baseline confirms that paging correlates with p99 tail spikes during bursts.

2024-09-18: sticky-reuse-window (prototype)
- Idea: mark keys with reuse_count>=2 within 10s as "sticky" and exempt from eviction until memory pressure crosses threshold.
- Config: sticky_threshold=2, sticky_window=10s, pressure_threshold=85% memory util.
- Observations: p99 reduced on synthetic workload from 310ms->210ms; during long bursts improved to 480ms. Eviction decreased by 18%. But tail improved inconsistently on real replay (small QPS windows created starvation of new keys).
- Notes: need fairness / aging for sticky keys. Add decay factor.

2024-09-22: bandwidth-aware-thresholds
- Idea: raise eviction aggressiveness when observed memory bandwidth is low; when bandwidth is near-saturated, reduce eviction rate to avoid triggering large IO reads (we saw larger evictions preceded page backfills).
- Config: bandwidth_high >= 85% => set eviction_batch_size = small; bandwidth_low <= 40% => larger batches allowed.
- Observations: when tuned, p95 improved 10-15% during mixed traffic; p99 similar but with fewer NVMe read bursts. However throughput dropped 3-5% due to more conservative churn.

2024-09-26: combined-policy (sticky + bandwidth-aware + decay)
- Config: sticky with decay tau=30s; bandwidth-aware thresholds; soft fairness by allowing forced eviction of oldest sticky after 60s.
- Observations: best of both worlds in synthetic tests: p99 down to 180ms steady, long-burst p99 around 420ms. Real replay saw fewer extreme read bursts. Eviction writes still high on sustained long sessions.

2024-09-30: dynamic-prefetching probe
- Idea: when eviction would evict a contiguous set of kv pages, prefetch high-likelihood victim neighborhood into DRAM (cheap reads) to amortize page faults if it will be reused soon. This is experimental and increases read IO but reduces major faults.
- Observations: reduced major page fault count by 36% in small runs; increased NVMe ops but with decreased latency tail. Risk: prefetch misprediction increases bandwidth and can worsen global saturation.

Correlation analyses (summary)

- Strong correlation between sudden rise in eviction volume and subsequent NVMe read bursts (Spearman rho ~0.68 on synthetic traces).
- Memory bandwidth saturation is a precursor for longer tail latency; peaks in bandwidth usage precede p99 spikes by ~200-800ms in most traces.
- Sticky keys reduce local rework but can cause new-key starvation unless decay is present.

Interesting micro-observations

- Eviction of contiguous memory ranges (page-aligned) is more expensive than scattered single-key evictions due to pageback behavior on NUMA nodes.
- When eviction policies select victims across multiple NUMA regions, pageback amplifies cross-node DMA and stalls other GPUs. Locality-aware eviction helped in small tests.

Open questions / hypotheses to validate

1) Can we make a light-weight per-epoch reuse histogram that lets us identify a small top-K hotset and protect it cheaply? (Tradeoff: histogram memory vs eviction savings).
2) Is a moving-median of bandwidth a better signal than instantaneous %util to decide eviction batch sizes?
3) Can small prefetch windows using async reads be safely limited by a global BW budget, preventing runaway prefetch?
4) How much of p99 is attributable to kernel-level page reclaim vs user-space rehydration cost? (Need syscall traces).

Planned next experiments

- 2024-10-05: implement top-K hotset sampler (approx-count sketch) and test with decay. Compare memory overhead and p99 improvement.
- 2024-10-09: NUMA-aware eviction prototype: prefer victims on same NUMA node as requesting GPU. Run microbench with cross-node traffic.
- 2024-10-14: Bandwidth median vs mean experiment: swap bandwidth signal to median-of-5s and rerun combined-policy tests.

Action items (owners)

- @Priya: instrument lightweight approximate-top-K hotset counter (prototype). Target: +PR by 2024-10-04.
- @Marco: add per-eviction event tagging with NUMA node and page alignment info (logs). Target: 2024-10-01.
- @Janelle: run larger production replay with sticky+decay settings and collect long-run stats (48h). Start 2024-10-06.
- @Ravi: evaluate async prefetch rate limiter; small throttle guard to cap BW impact. Proof-of-concept due 2024-10-11.

Notes to self / experimentation heuristics

- Always run paired-control tests: same seed traffic with only one variable changed.
- Save raw perf-counters and eviction traces for at least 48 hours after a test.
- When in doubt, prioritize small conservative changes (soft guards) that favor availability over raw throughput.

Concluding thoughts (so far)

Combining short-term reuse signals with bandwidth-aware eviction settings seems promising: we can reduce p99 tails and NVMe read bursts without massive complexity. Biggest dangers are fairness (sticky keys starving new contexts) and runaway prefetch. Next milestone is to validate the approximate-top-K approach at scale and to add NUMA-awareness for eviction selection.

References and links

- JIRA: JIRA-RT-842 (eviction heuristics spiking tail latency).
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/678 (experiment harness changes).

-- Evan L.
